Record · Walter Hines Page
A house
directed from London.
Garran Hill · 1916
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918
He named it Garran Hill.
The life he imagined happened elsewhere.

In February 1913, he bought a thousand-acre farm on land his father had logged a generation earlier. He gave it a name before the first stone was laid: Garran Hill.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game."

Weeks later, Wilson offered him London. The ambassadorship to the Court of St. James's. Page accepted — and left. He directed the making of the house by letter, from three thousand miles away, while his son Ralph carried the work on the ground.

When he finally reached Pinehurst in December 1918, the house was finished. He stayed at Currituck Cottage — not Garran Hill — and died there ten days later. He never slept a single night in the house he had spent five years building.

"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?" — Walter Hines Page, Aberdeen station, December 11, 1918
The Craftsmen · 1915–1916
Flemish bond brick. White portico.
A circular lawn held before the entrance like a pause.
Leonard Tufts · Boston Plans · Pinehurst Hands

The plans came from Boston.
The character came from here.

Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen — the same men building Pinehurst. What they laid into this house is still there. Flemish bond brickwork across the entire facade: alternating headers and stretchers, the signature pattern of Georgian masonry, a level of precision most builders no longer attempt. A water table at the first-floor base still throwing rain off the foundation. A belt course at the second-floor transition, exactly as drawn in 1916.

Dentil molding along the cornice under the pediment. Leaded glass sidelights. A semicircular fanlight with its original radial tracery still intact. Herringbone brick at the threshold. Original oak floors throughout. A mahogany volute on the staircase that still turns with the authority of a signature.

Flemish bond · water table · belt course · dentil molding · fanlight · leaded glass · herringbone brick · mahogany volute · 1915–1916
The Entry

Doric columns.
A fanlight that has held its glass since 1916.

The portico is not ornament. It is proportion. Four Doric columns, a pediment, and a semicircular fanlight with its original radial tracery. Dentil molding runs the full cornice. The brick steps continue the Flemish bond of the facade without interruption. Floor, riser, landing, wall — all the same hand.

The belt course marks the first-to-second-floor transition exactly as drawn. The water table sits where it has always sat, throwing rain off the foundation since 1916.

This is what Leonard Tufts's men left. Not a house trying to look like 1916. A house that has simply never stopped being 1916.

“The friend of Britain
in her sorest need.”
Westminster Abbey tablet for Walter Hines Page
Garran Hill · 1916
The door has been open since 1916.
Inlaid in the threshold brick. Not branding. Not nostalgia. Evidence — laid into the house before anyone knew what the house would outlive.
Restoration Record · 1998–2001

Fourteen quiet years.
Then the house was believed again.

After Betty Dumaine's death, the house stood vacant for roughly fourteen years.

The current stewards purchased the house in 1998 and restored it with the rare discipline of people who understood the assignment: not reinvention, but custody.

The restoration record includes architectural drawings, repaired oak floors, revived details, a kitchen built in the language of the old house, and the crucial refusal to make the place newly clever.

Original

Oak floors, threshold, leaded glass, brass key plates, staircase volute, carved mantels, and the surviving architectural rhythm of 1916.

Restored

Rooms returned to proportion, systems renewed, and details repaired without sanding the soul off the house.

Added Carefully

The kitchen: not original to 1916, but original to the restoration — practical and honest about its date.

The Staircase
The mahogany volute.
Still turning with the authority of a signature.

The volute at the base of the staircase was hand-carved in 1916. The original keys are still in every plate on every door off this hall.

The Drawing Room
Fire going.
No one home yet.

The mantel is carved white wood. Georgian in proportion. The blue and white Delft tile surround is hand-painted, original to 1916. The coffered ceiling was enlarged during construction. They made it bigger so they could dance.

The Salon
Someone still
puts flowers there.

The room has been in use for a hundred years without interruption. Original oak floors. A fireplace that has not missed a winter since 1916. This is where Betty Dumaine received the world she had made.

The Dining Room
Formal by proportion.
Intimate by firelight.

A curved north bay looks directly onto the grounds. Arched shell alcoves flank the fireplace with scalloped tops and built-in cabinets below. The table seats twelve. The third of seven fireplaces in the house.

The Library
The books stayed.

The spiral stair rises to a second floor of shelves. Two walls of light. Its own fireplace. Whoever built this room intended to disappear into it.

The Kitchen
Not original to 1916.
Original to the restoration.

Reclaimed heart-pine floors. Two farm sinks. A butler's pantry. A wall of divided-light windows facing the grounds. It does not pretend to be 1916. That is why it belongs.

The Primary Suite
Drapes drawn.
Window latch, closed.

Four-poster bed. Afternoon light at the edges of the drapes. A room that has the particular stillness of a place that has been slept in for a long time by people who were glad to be there.

The Jewel Box
Fuchsia chinoiserie.
Water taps wait.

The name is not ours — it is what the room earns. Brass taps. A tasseled sink skirt. The kind of bathroom that stops a conversation mid-sentence when the guest walks in.

4.15 Acres · Pinehurst, North Carolina
In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.
The present 4.15 acres are the original house parcel of Page's larger farm. The grounds carry the long evidence of human intention: camellias, magnolias, dogwoods, American plane trees, and shade that has had a century to become itself.
Not the whole thousand acres. The part that remembers.
Blue Fox · 1946–1965
Someone still
puts flowers there.

At the back of the grounds, beneath a slate cover with a brass marker, Betty Dumaine buried Blue Fox — her Irish hunter.

The marker remains. So, impossibly, do the flowers.

Blue Fox — My Irish Hunter — 1946 to 1965.
Hollycrest · Back of the property · Under a slate cover with a brass marker
Hollycrest · 1959–1984

She renamed it Hollycrest.
Then gave it a second world.

Elizabeth “Betty” Dumaine purchased the house in 1959 and gave it the name Hollycrest — a name still preserved, quietly and stubbornly, in 200 Hollycrest Drive.

At nineteen, Betty attended the Edith Johnson School in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where her roommate was Khun Sangwan Chukramol. Sangwan later married Prince Mahidol of Songkla and became Srinagarindra, Princess Mother of Thailand.

From Pinehurst, Betty supported the Princess Mother's charitable work in Northern Thailand. She raised funds, founded a riding club, kept horses and hounds, and gave the grounds their second great life.

Her version of stewardship was not quiet in the small sense. It had peacocks, gardens, horses, charity, ceremony, and one little grave at the back of the grounds that still knows how to break your heart.

The Record

The record is not thin.

The record is not atmosphere. It is documentation.

Page's letters. PineStraw's account. The Village Heritage Foundation's landmark record. Westminster Abbey's inscription. TPMCF's biography of Betty Dumaine.

The story still has a threshold, a stair, a key in the lock, and a door that opens.
